section: Rural, urban and tribal society in India - features and interlinkages
subsections: Urban problems - slums, housing, pollution, crime; link to industrialisation
Tribal society - features vs peasant society, tribal-rural transitions
Migration linkages - rural-urban migration, footloose labour, informal labour
Andhra Pradesh - rural/urban/tribal shares and urban centres

accepted.s: Industrialisation generally drives urbanisation primarily by:
o: Creating employment opportunities in urban areas
Reducing rural population through compulsory relocation
accepted.x: Industrialisation creates jobs in towns and cities, thereby encouraging urbanisation. Rural-to-urban migration is its main demographic component.
accepted.tq: Identify the direct cause-and-effect relationship rather than choosing an extreme consequence.
accepted.sec: Urban problems - slums, housing, pollution, crime; link to industrialisation  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a consequence of rapid urbanisation?
o: Strengthening of traditional social control in all urban settlements
Rising crime associated with population density
accepted.x: Rapid urbanisation may weaken social control and produce maladjustment, crime, environmental degradation and alienation; it does not universally strengthen traditional social control.
accepted.tq: Find the option that reverses the stated urban trend.
accepted.sec: Urban problems - slums, housing, pollution, crime; link to industrialisation  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding urban problems:
1. High population density can be associated with rising crime.
2. Urbanisation may produce maladjustment.
3. Urban settlements may display visible segregation between rich and poor.
4. Urbanisation eliminates social alienation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because alienation is among the problems associated with urbanisation.
accepted.tq: Reject the statement using an absolute reversal of a listed urban problem.
accepted.sec: Urban problems - slums, housing, pollution, crime; link to industrialisation  [other exams]

accepted.s: In the context of urbanisation, informality comprising slums, informal labour and unregistered firms is regarded as:
o: A consequence only of tribal isolation
A feature confined to rural economies
A structural outcome of rapid urbanisation requiring integration
A temporary phenomenon that must be eradicated completely
accepted.x: The Economic Survey 2025-26 perspective treats informality as a structural outcome of rapid urbanisation that should be integrated rather than eradicated.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the policy approach of integration from the misleading extreme of eradication.
accepted.sec: Urban problems - slums, housing, pollution, crime; link to industrialisation  [other exams]

accepted.s: Why do many low-income workers choose informal housing close to employment centres?
o: Informal housing always provides superior public services
Workers are prohibited from living in formal housing
Formal affordable housing on the periphery often lacks connectivity
Employment centres are generally located in villages
accepted.x: Low-income workers often prefer informal housing near jobs because formal affordable housing on the urban periphery may not have adequate connectivity.
accepted.tq: Apply the housing-location relationship to a realistic urban scenario.
accepted.sec: Urban problems - slums, housing, pollution, crime; link to industrialisation  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which institutional condition aggravates urban governance problems by limiting the capacity of cities to respond independently?
o: Complete integration of all urban agencies
Institutional fragmentation and lack of fiscal autonomy
accepted.x: Cities often lack fiscal autonomy, and institutional fragmentation further complicates urban governance.
accepted.tq: Match the governance problem with the institutional cause stated in precise terms.
accepted.sec: Urban problems - slums, housing, pollution, crime; link to industrialisation  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Caste continues to influence urban social life through:
1. Concentration of particular castes in slums
2. Residential segregation
3. Caste networks for obtaining employment
4. Complete disappearance of caste identities in cities
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Caste persists in cities through slum concentration, residential segregation and caste-based employment networks. Its complete disappearance is incorrect.
accepted.tq: Separate the three concrete mechanisms from the absolute claim that caste disappears.
accepted.sec: Urban problems - slums, housing, pollution, crime; link to industrialisation  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature associated with tribal society?
o: Highly individualised land ownership linked to tenancy markets
accepted.x: Tribal society is characterised by communal control of land and forests, whereas individual land ownership and tenancy are associated with peasant society.
accepted.tq: Use the tribe-peasant contrast to identify the misplaced feature.
accepted.sec: Tribal society - features vs peasant society, tribal-rural transitions

accepted.s: The Imperial Gazetteer described a tribe as families having a common:
o: Landlord, tenancy system and village council
Caste rank, occupation and market association
Political party, religion and language script
accepted.x: The Imperial Gazetteer description emphasised families with a common name, dialect and territory, and originally endogamous organisation.
accepted.tq: Recall the exact three-part descriptive formulation.
accepted.sec: Tribal society - features vs peasant society, tribal-rural transitions

accepted.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Tribal society — stratified primarily by caste and class
Peasant society — relatively isolated and kinship-based
Tribal society — subsistence economy and common control of land and forest
Peasant society — absence of market linkages
accepted.x: Tribal society is relatively isolated and kinship-based, with a subsistence economy and common control of land and forest. Peasant society is part of a wider, caste- and class-stratified, market-linked society with individual land and tenancy.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure contrast between communal tribal resources and individual peasant landholding.
accepted.sec: Tribal society - features vs peasant society, tribal-rural transitions

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about tribal society:
1. It may have a common name and dialect.
2. Animism or totemism may be present.
3. Youth dormitories are among its noted institutional features.
4. Its economy is necessarily complex and industrialised.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Common name and dialect, animism or totemism, youth dormitories and a simple economy are listed tribal features. A necessarily industrialised economy is incorrect.
accepted.tq: Test several descriptive features while rejecting the exaggerated economic characterization.
accepted.sec: Tribal society - features vs peasant society, tribal-rural transitions

accepted.s: Who associated the gradual assimilation of tribes with the ‘Hindu method of tribal absorption’?
accepted.x: N.K. Bose used the expression ‘Hindu method of tribal absorption’ to describe gradual assimilation.
accepted.tq: Use the thinker-concept association and avoid confusing it with the other transition theories.
accepted.sec: Tribal society - features vs peasant society, tribal-rural transitions

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Scholar)
A. N.K. Bose
B. Surajit Sinha
C. T.K. Oommen

List-II (Concept)
1. Tribal autonomy movements
2. Hindu method of tribal absorption
3. Tribe-caste continuum and secondary state formation

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: N.K. Bose is associated with the Hindu method of tribal absorption; Surajit Sinha with tribe-caste continuum and secondary state formation; and T.K. Oommen with tribal autonomy movements.
accepted.tq: Start from the distinctive scholar-concept pair and eliminate codes containing a swapped association.
accepted.sec: Tribal society - features vs peasant society, tribal-rural transitions

accepted.s: According to Census 2011, Scheduled Tribes constituted what percentage of India’s population?
accepted.x: Scheduled Tribes constituted 8.6% of India’s population in Census 2011, numbering 10.43 crore.
accepted.tq: Separate the percentage share from the population count and growth-rate figures.
accepted.sec: Tribal society - features vs peasant society, tribal-rural transitions

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly represents the rural-urban distribution of India’s Scheduled Tribe population according to Census 2011?
accepted.x: According to Census 2011, 89.97% of the Scheduled Tribe population was rural and 10.03% was urban.
accepted.tq: Watch for the rural and urban percentages being deliberately reversed.
accepted.sec: Tribal society - features vs peasant society, tribal-rural transitions

accepted.s:
With reference to Scheduled Tribes in Census 2011, consider the following statements:
1. Their decadal growth rate was 23.66%.
2. The all-India decadal growth rate was 17.69%.
3. Their sex ratio was 990, compared with the all-India figure of 940.
4. The number of recognised ST groups was 705.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All four statements are correct: the ST decadal growth rate was 23.66%, the all-India rate was 17.69%, the ST sex ratio was 990 against 940 overall, and 705 ST groups were recorded.
accepted.tq: Retain the complete numerical cluster and distinguish growth, sex ratio and group-count measures.
accepted.sec: Tribal society - features vs peasant society, tribal-rural transitions

accepted.s: Migration, in the demographic sense used in this context, refers to:
o: Only international movement across national borders
Seasonal movement without any change of residence
Any daily movement within the same locality
A change of residence between areas for a considerable period
accepted.x: Migration is defined as a change of residence between areas for a considerable period; it is not limited to international movement.
accepted.tq: Distinguish a change of residence from routine commuting or short-term movement.
accepted.sec: Migration linkages - rural-urban migration, footloose labour, informal labour

accepted.s: The principal source States of rural-to-urban migrants identified in this context are:
accepted.x: Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are identified as the main source States of migrants.
accepted.tq: Recall the specific source-State pair rather than choosing major destination States.
accepted.sec: Migration linkages - rural-urban migration, footloose labour, informal labour

accepted.s: Which of the following is a push factor for rural-to-urban migration?
o: Improved formal housing connectivity in cities
accepted.x: Monsoon failure and rural unemployment push people away from rural areas towards urban employment opportunities.
accepted.tq: Identify the condition that pushes migrants out of the place of origin.
accepted.sec: Migration linkages - rural-urban migration, footloose labour, informal labour

accepted.s: Urban wages are estimated to be approximately how many times rural wages?
accepted.x: Urban wages are reported to be about 1.7 to 2 times rural wages.
accepted.tq: Select the stated range and avoid inflating the comparative figure.
accepted.sec: Migration linkages - rural-urban migration, footloose labour, informal labour

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements regarding rural conditions and migration is correct?
o: About 35% of rural households lack quality healthcare within 5 km, and migration may leave ageing parents behind.
About 65% of Indians are urban, and migration generally leaves no family members behind.
Quality healthcare within 5 km is unavailable to nearly all rural households.
Migration is unrelated to the availability of rural healthcare.
accepted.x: About 35% of rural households lack quality healthcare within 5 km, and migration can leave ageing parents behind. Around 65% of Indians remain rural.
accepted.tq: Choose the precise combined statement while rejecting reversed or exaggerated proportions.
accepted.sec: Migration linkages - rural-urban migration, footloose labour, informal labour

accepted.s: The term ‘footloose labour’, as used by Jan Breman, refers to:
o: Circular migrant workers moving among seasonal, casual and informal jobs
Highly skilled workers employed permanently by multinational firms
Permanent agricultural labourers tied to one village
accepted.x: Jan Breman’s Footloose Labour (1996) describes circular migrant workers who move between seasonal, casual and informal employment.
accepted.tq: Match the author and title with the exact labour-mobility concept.
accepted.sec: Migration linkages - rural-urban migration, footloose labour, informal labour

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about female labour force participation:
1. The FLFPR for persons aged 15 years and above rose from 30% in 2019-20 to 40% in 2025.
2. Rural FLFPR rose from 33% to 45.9%.
3. Urban FLFPR rose from 23.3% to 27.7%.
4. Urban FLFPR increased more than rural FLFPR in absolute percentage points.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Rural FLFPR increased by 12.9 percentage points, while urban FLFPR increased by 4.4 points, so statement 4 is false.
accepted.tq: Compare both the levels and the absolute changes before selecting the coded combination.
accepted.sec: Migration linkages - rural-urban migration, footloose labour, informal labour

accepted.s: The objective phrase associated with the Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission is:
accepted.x: The Rurban Mission, launched in 2016, is associated with the objective ‘rural soul, urban amenities’.
accepted.tq: Recall the official programme phrase along with its rural-urban orientation.
accepted.sec: Migration linkages - rural-urban migration, footloose labour, informal labour

accepted.s: Which organisation is associated with implementation of the Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP)?
accepted.x: PMEGP is implemented through the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC).
accepted.tq: Use the implementing-body trap by distinguishing the employment agency from urban and census authorities.
accepted.sec: Migration linkages - rural-urban migration, footloose labour, informal labour

accepted.s: According to the 2011 data cited for Andhra Pradesh, the State’s urban population share was:
accepted.x: Andhra Pradesh had an urban share of 29.47% in 2011, up from 24.13% in 2001, leaving about 70.5% rural.
accepted.tq: Check both the current value and the direction of change instead of reversing the years.
accepted.sec: Andhra Pradesh - rural/urban/tribal shares and urban centres

accepted.s: Which districts were identified as the most urbanised in Andhra Pradesh according to the 2011 figures cited?
accepted.x: Visakhapatnam, with 47.45% urbanisation, and Krishna, with 40.81%, were the most urbanised districts in the cited 2011 figures.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the highest pair from the least-urbanised districts and later reorganisation data.
accepted.sec: Andhra Pradesh - rural/urban/tribal shares and urban centres

accepted.s: Which pair represents the least urbanised districts in Andhra Pradesh according to the cited 2011 figures?
accepted.x: Srikakulam had 16.16% urbanisation and Prakasam 19.56%, making them the least urbanised among the cited districts.
accepted.tq: Match the district pair with the lower percentage range rather than the later 2025 reorganisation figures.
accepted.sec: Andhra Pradesh - rural/urban/tribal shares and urban centres

accepted.s: After the 2025 reorganisation into 28 districts, which district had the highest urbanisation according to the cited analysis?
accepted.x: After the 2025 reorganisation, Visakhapatnam had the highest urbanisation at 89.69%. Polavaram had the lowest at 2.84%.
accepted.tq: Keep the pre-reorganisation and post-reorganisation district comparisons separate.
accepted.sec: Andhra Pradesh - rural/urban/tribal shares and urban centres

accepted.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched after Andhra Pradesh’s 2025 district reorganisation?
accepted.x: Polavaram had the lowest urbanisation at 2.84%, while Visakhapatnam had the highest at 89.69%. Polavaram and Markapuram were the new districts mentioned.
accepted.tq: Use the reversed comparison trap involving highest and lowest values.
accepted.sec: Andhra Pradesh - rural/urban/tribal shares and urban centres

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about Scheduled Tribes in Andhra Pradesh:
1. They numbered 27.39 lakh according to the 2011 data.
2. They constituted 5.53% of the State’s population.
3. Andhra Pradesh had 34 Scheduled Tribe communities.
4. All Scheduled Tribe population lived within Scheduled Areas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because about 12.9 lakh tribals lived in the Scheduled Areas, not the entire tribal population of 27.39 lakh.
accepted.tq: Test the difference between the total tribal population and the population residing in Scheduled Areas.
accepted.sec: Andhra Pradesh - rural/urban/tribal shares and urban centres

accepted.s: The Scheduled Areas of Andhra Pradesh covered approximately:
accepted.x: Scheduled Areas covered 16,267.63 square kilometres, approximately 10.15% of Andhra Pradesh, and included 3,512 villages.
accepted.tq: Distinguish area, percentage and village-count units, which are deliberately interchangeable traps.
accepted.sec: Andhra Pradesh - rural/urban/tribal shares and urban centres

accepted.s: Scheduled Areas in Andhra Pradesh extend across which of the following districts?
o: Parvathipuram Manyam, Vizianagaram, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Anakapalli and Eluru
Visakhapatnam, Krishna, Srikakulam, Prakasam and Markapuram only
Polavaram, Krishna, Guntur, Nellore and Kurnool
accepted.x: The cited Scheduled Areas include villages in Parvathipuram Manyam, Vizianagaram, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Anakapalli and Eluru districts.
accepted.tq: Match the complete geographical list and reject options that substitute urbanisation districts or all districts.
accepted.sec: Andhra Pradesh - rural/urban/tribal shares and urban centres

accepted.s: Approximately how many tribal people live in the Scheduled Areas of Andhra Pradesh?
accepted.x: About 12.9 lakh tribals live in the Scheduled Areas, compared with 27.39 lakh Scheduled Tribes in the State as a whole.
accepted.tq: Separate the population living in Scheduled Areas from the total tribal population of the State.
accepted.sec: Andhra Pradesh - rural/urban/tribal shares and urban centres

accepted.s: How many panchayats in Andhra Pradesh were classified under the Rurban cluster scheme?
accepted.x: A total of 359 panchayats in Andhra Pradesh were classified under the Rurban cluster scheme.
accepted.tq: Match the scheme with its panchayat count rather than the ULB or Scheduled Area figures.
accepted.sec: Andhra Pradesh - rural/urban/tribal shares and urban centres

accepted.s: Which authority was reported to have told a parliamentary panel that the Census Town definition is outdated?
o: Office of the Registrar General of India
Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
accepted.x: The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs told the parliamentary panel headed by TDP MP Magunta Sreenivasulu Reddy that the Census Town definition is outdated.
accepted.tq: Use the ‘who said what’ authority trap in an institutional context.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: What is the stated position of the Registrar General of India regarding the Census Town definition?
o: It has abolished the definition immediately for all purposes.
It is retaining the definition for Census 2027.
It is applying the definition only to Scheduled Areas.
It has transferred the definition to the Election Commission.
accepted.x: Although the Census Town definition was criticised as outdated, the Registrar General of India is retaining it for Census 2027.
accepted.tq: Distinguish criticism of a definition from the administrative decision to retain it temporarily.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: The parliamentary panel associated with the discussion on the Census Town definition was headed by:
accepted.x: The parliamentary panel was headed by TDP Member of Parliament Magunta Sreenivasulu Reddy.
accepted.tq: Identify the institutional office-holder rather than the scholars linked to tribal studies.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: Why is the rural-urban binary criticised in discussions of rapidly urbanising areas?
o: It prevents any rural area from receiving public funds.
It classifies every village as a statutory town.
It places such areas under panchayats that may have limited fiscal power.
It gives all rapidly urbanising areas complete municipal autonomy.
accepted.x: The rural-urban binary may leave rapidly urbanising areas under panchayats with limited fiscal power, creating a governance mismatch.
accepted.tq: Apply the classification problem to the institutional consequence for fast-urbanising areas.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly compares Andhra Pradesh with the national average in urbanisation?
o: AP is less urbanised: 29.47% against the national 31.16%.
AP is less urbanised: 24.13% against the national 31.16%.
AP is more urbanised: 31.16% against the national 29.47%.
Both have exactly the same urban share.
accepted.x: Andhra Pradesh’s urbanisation share was 29.47%, lower than the national average of 31.16%. Its urbanisation is concentrated particularly in Visakhapatnam and Krishna.
accepted.tq: Check both sides of the comparison and avoid substituting AP’s 2001 figure for its 2011 figure.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: Which pair best describes the spatial pattern of urbanisation in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Concentrated exclusively in Srikakulam and Prakasam
accepted.x: Andhra Pradesh is less urbanised than the national average, and its urbanisation is concentrated in Visakhapatnam and Krishna.
accepted.tq: Identify the broad spatial pattern rather than choosing the least-urbanised districts.
accepted.sec: Universal angles
